I will keep my full 20 mu in the wheat-maize rotation because that fits my land, my irrigation condition, and the way my family works. Some people in my household work off-farm, so I will choose a management style that is steady and not too risky. For wheat, I will use improved seed rather than traditional seed because I want more stable emergence, better disease resistance, and a reliable yield on irrigated land. I will put in a moderate amount of fertilizer, with nitrogen as the main input and enough phosphorus and potassium to support root growth and grain filling. Since I have well irrigation, I will irrigate wheat several times at the key stages because wheat responds well to water here and I do not want to lose yield from spring drought. I will use rotary tillage after the maize season because it is practical for my scale and helps me prepare the seedbed without taking too much time. I will spray pesticides only as much as needed to control the common problems and avoid wasting money.

For maize, I will also stay with improved or hybrid seed because I care most about stable output from my summer crop. After wheat harvest, I will get the maize in quickly so the season is not delayed. Maize needs nitrogen, but I will keep the fertilizer rate balanced because too much only raises cost and lodging risk. With well irrigation, I can support the crop if summer rain is uneven, but I will not irrigate more than necessary because maize in this system usually gets part of its water from rainfall. I will keep rotary tillage for convenience and labor saving. Overall, I am aiming for solid yields from both crops with controlled costs, because with 20 mu and some off-farm work in the family, I value dependable returns more than chasing the absolute highest output.
